statement: Value iteration for stochastic games (Algorithm 6) converges to the unique optimal value functions V*_i because the update operator of Equation 6.4 is a gamma-contraction mapping under the max-norm, so repeated application converges to a unique fixed point by the Banach fixed-point theorem.
section: 6.1 Dynamic Programming for Games: Value Iteration
conditions: zero-sum, two-agent stochastic game; Valuei computed as the minimax value of the per-state normal-form game; discount factor gamma in [0,1)
limits: proof sketch summarized in text, full derivation attributed to Shapley (1953); established only for the two-agent zero-sum case, though the algorithm template is suggested (not proved) to generalize

statement: The value iteration algorithm for stochastic games reduces exactly to standard MDP value iteration in the single-agent special case, since the minimax Valuei operator collapses to a max-operator over a single agent's action values.
section: 6.1 Dynamic Programming for Games: Value Iteration
conditions: single-agent stochastic game (i.e., an MDP)
limits: a consistency check for the N=1 boundary case only; does not itself bear on behavior for N>2 agents

statement: Minimax Q-learning is guaranteed to learn the unique minimax value of a two-agent zero-sum stochastic game, provided all combinations of states and joint actions are tried infinitely often and the usual learning-rate conditions from single-agent RL hold.
conditions: two-agent zero-sum stochastic games; infinite visitation of all state/joint-action pairs; standard Robbins-Monro-style learning-rate schedule
limits: convergence result attributed externally to Littman and Szepesvari (1996), not proved in this text; applies only to two-agent zero-sum games

statement: In a simplified two-agent zero-sum soccer game, a policy learned by minimax Q-learning won 53.7% of episodes against a hand-built opponent (close to the theoretical 50%) and 37.5% against an optimal worst-case opponent, while independent Q-learning won 76.3% against the hand-built opponent (by exploiting its weaknesses) but 0% against the optimal opponent.
evidence_type: empirical figure reproduced from cited paper
conditions: 4x5 grid-world soccer game, two agents, one million training time steps, exploration rate epsilon=0.2, initial learning rate alpha=1.0 decayed by factor 0.9999954 per step, discount gamma=0.9, tested over 100,000 time steps per opponent type; results reproduced from Littman (1994)
limits: single task/environment (grid-world soccer); results are from the original 1994 paper, not an independent replication by these authors

statement: Nash Q-learning converges to a Nash equilibrium of a general-sum stochastic game only if, in addition to infinite exploration of state/joint-action pairs and standard learning-rate conditions, every normal-form game encountered during learning consistently has either (a) a global optimum for all agents or (b) a saddle point.
conditions: general-sum stochastic games, any finite number of agents; every per-state normal-form game Gamma_s must have a global optimum in all encountered games, or a saddle point in all encountered games (not merely some)
limits: the authors state this condition is 'highly restrictive' and unlikely to hold in any encountered game, let alone all of them

statement: The book's Nash Q-learning convergence guarantee is conditioned on every per-state game encountered during learning satisfying the global-optimum-or-saddle-point structural property; this restrictive-condition guarantee is not evidence that Nash Q-learning converges in general N-agent stochastic games lacking that property.
conditions: n/a (curator-stated boundary on interpretation)
limits: bounded to the inspected text's own stated conditions for Nash Q-learning

statement: The text states explicitly that no formal conditions are known under which correlated Q-learning converges to a correlated equilibrium of the stochastic game.
conditions: general-sum stochastic games with a finite number of agents, correlated equilibrium solved via linear programming per state
limits: this is an explicit non-result stated by the authors, not a proved negative result; correlated Q-learning's two claimed benefits (wider solution space, cheaper LP-based computation) are asserted without a convergence guarantee

statement: For any NoSDE game with a unique equilibrium joint policy, there exists another NoSDE game differing only in the reward functions, with its own unique equilibrium policy, such that the two games share identical equilibrium joint-action value functions for every agent, yet the two equilibrium policies yield different expected returns (value functions) for at least one agent.
conditions: class of NoSDE ('No Stationary Deterministic Equilibrium') turn-taking stochastic games, i.e., only one agent has more than one available action in any given state, and the game's unique stationary equilibrium is probabilistic rather than deterministic
limits: theorem attributed to Zinkevich, Greenwald, and Littman (2005); proof is not reproduced in this text; equation_text_unreliable flags the rendering of Equation 6.12

statement: The NoSDE theorem is demonstrated via a specific small (two-state, two-agent, deterministic-transition) counterexample construction; it establishes that joint-action value functions can be insufficient for equilibrium recovery in at least this game class, not that all state-conditioned joint-action-value algorithms fail to recover equilibria on all stochastic games, nor does it address scaling behavior with agent count N.
conditions: n/a (curator-stated boundary on interpretation)
limits: bounded to the inspected NoSDE construction and its stated theorem

statement: Joint-action learning with agent modeling (JAL-AM, Algorithm 8) does not require the learning agent to observe the rewards of other agents and maintains only a single joint-action value function Qi for the learning agent, in contrast to JAL-GT algorithms, which require observing all agents' rewards each time step and maintaining a joint-action value function Qj for every agent.
conditions: stochastic games with full state and joint-action observability; the modeling agent must still observe the actions (not rewards) of other agents to update its models
limits: reduced information requirement relative to JAL-GT is stated as a structural property of the algorithm design, not as an empirically measured cost/benefit trade-off

statement: In the level-based foraging task, JAL-AM converged (on average, over fifty independent training runs) to the optimal joint policy after about 500,000 training time steps and with lower variance in evaluation returns than independent Q-learning (IQL) and central Q-learning (CQL), while IQL required about 600,000 training time steps to converge to the optimal joint policy.
conditions: level-based foraging task (from Figure 5.3); constant learning rate alpha=0.01; exploration rate linearly decayed from 1 to 0.05 over the first 80,000 time steps; fifty independent training runs, shaded standard deviation reported
limits: single task (level-based foraging); IQL and CQL curves copied from an earlier figure (5.4) rather than rerun alongside JAL-AM in this experiment

statement: Because fictitious play's best response (Equation 6.15) selects a single deterministic optimal action rather than a policy, fictitious play cannot itself learn equilibrium solutions that require randomization, such as the uniform-random Nash equilibrium of Rock-Paper-Scissors; however, the empirical distribution of the agents' past actions can converge to such randomized equilibria.
conditions: non-repeated normal-form games; each agent models others via the empirical distribution of past actions (Equation 6.14)
limits: distinguishes the non-convergence of the played policy from the convergence of the empirical action distribution; the latter's convergence is stated to hold only in certain game classes, not universally

statement: In a worked repeated Prisoner's Dilemma example with a uniform prior belief over two candidate models of the other agent (Coop, Grim), an agent using value-of-information (VI) best responses computes VI(cooperate) = -9 and VI(defect) = -13.5 in the initial time step, so both agents following VI will cooperate initially and continue cooperating until defecting in the final (end-game) time step.
section: 6.3.3 Bayesian Learning and Value of Information
conditions: repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, ten time steps per episode, uniform prior 0.5/0.5 over Coop and Grim opponent models, no discounting (gamma=1), VI recursion depth equal to episode length (10)
limits: specific to this prior, discount factor, recursion depth, and two-model candidate space; the authors note elsewhere that the choice of prior belief can substantially affect achievable returns and convergence

statement: A central result in rational learning states that, under certain strict assumptions including 'absolute continuity' (any history with positive probability under the agents' actual policies must have positive probability under the agents' beliefs), agents' predictions of future play converge to the true distribution of play and the agents' policies converge to a Nash equilibrium.
section: 6.3.3 Bayesian Learning and Value of Information
conditions: Bayesian belief updating over a space of candidate agent models; the absolute-continuity assumption must hold, i.e., the true best-response behavior of other agents must be predictable by some model in the candidate model space
limits: attributed to Kalai and Lehrer (1993), not proved in this text; the authors show with a skewed prior example (0.8 Coop / 0.2 Grim) that absolute continuity can be violated, producing behavior (mutual initial defection) not predicted by either candidate model

statement: The gradient-ascent policy-learning method of Section 6.4.1 requires each agent to know its own reward matrix exactly and to observe the other agent's current policy in the current episode when computing its gradient update.
conditions: two-agent, two-action, general-sum non-repeated normal-form games
limits: the authors state a generalization (GIGA, Section 6.4.5) relaxes the need to know the other agent's policy, requiring only observation of its realized past actions

statement: The gradient-ascent method of Section 6.4.1 and the IGA convergence analysis of Section 6.4.2 assume each agent has full knowledge of its own reward matrix and either the exact current policy (IGA) or the realized actions (GIGA) of the other agent; this full/near-full information setting is not evidence that these convergence results transfer to settings with unknown reward structure or a variable/unobserved set of co-agents.
conditions: n/a (curator-stated boundary on interpretation)
limits: bounded to the inspected sections' stated knowledge assumptions

statement: WoLF-IGA is guaranteed to converge to a Nash equilibrium in general-sum normal-form games with two agents and two actions, including the case where the underlying IGA dynamics would instead cycle indefinitely on an ellipse (purely imaginary eigenvalues with the center point inside the unit square).
conditions: two-agent, two-action, general-sum normal-form games; variable learning rate alternating between lmin (winning) and lmax (losing) per the WoLF principle
limits: attributed to Bowling and Veloso (2002), not proved in this text; restricted to the two-agent, two-action case

statement: Unlike WoLF-IGA, which is stated to provably converge to a Nash equilibrium in the two-agent two-action case, the text presents WoLF-PHC (Section 6.4.4) with only an informal justification (the averaged own-policy 'replaces' the unknown equilibrium policy, by analogy to fictitious play) and an empirical demonstration on Rock-Paper-Scissors; no formal Nash-equilibrium convergence theorem for WoLF-PHC itself is stated in this text.
section: 6.4.4 Win or Learn Fast with Policy Hill Climbing
conditions: n/a (curator-stated boundary on interpretation)
limits: bounded to the inspected section; a formal WoLF-PHC convergence result may exist in the cited original paper (Bowling and Veloso 2002) but is not reproduced or cited as a theorem in this chapter

statement: GIGA achieves no-regret: with step size kappa_k = 1/sqrt(k), the regret of an agent using GIGA is bounded by Regret^k_i <= [sqrt(k) + (sqrt(k)-1)/2] * |Ai| * r_max^2, so the average regret goes to zero as k approaches infinity, and this no-regret property implies the empirical action distribution converges to a coarse correlated equilibrium; the result also implies IGA achieves no-regret, and extends to games with more than two agents by replacing the single opponent with the joint action of all other agents.
conditions: normal-form games, step size kappa_k = 1/sqrt(k), GIGA requires observing only the realized past actions of other agents (not their policies)
limits: attributed to Zinkevich (2003), not proved in this text; equation_text_unreliable flags the rendering of Equation 6.52 and surrounding text

statement: For both unconditional and conditional regret matching, each agent's average regret is bounded by kappa/sqrt(z) for some constant kappa>0, independent of the behavior of the other agents; as the number of episodes z goes to infinity, this bound implies the empirical distribution of joint actions converges to the set of coarse correlated equilibria (unconditional variant) or correlated equilibria (conditional variant), but does not imply pointwise convergence of the agents' actual policies to any equilibrium.
conditions: normal-form games; regret bound attributed to Hart and Mas-Colell (2000) and ultimately to Blackwell's Approachability Theorem (1956); holds regardless of other agents' action choices
limits: convergence is explicitly of the empirical action distribution, not of the actual policies pi^z_i, which the text illustrates (Figure 6.14) can remain non-convergent even as the empirical distribution converges; equation_text_unreliable flags Equations 6.59-6.64

statement: Regret matching's proven convergence guarantee (Section 6.5.2) is convergence of the empirical joint-action distribution to a (coarse) correlated equilibrium set, not convergence of the agents' actual played policies to a single equilibrium; this is a materially weaker convergence type than WoLF-PHC's or WoLF-IGA's stated pointwise policy convergence, and citations of 'regret matching converges to equilibrium' should preserve this distinction.
conditions: n/a (curator-stated boundary on interpretation)
limits: bounded to the inspected sections' explicit statements distinguishing empirical-distribution convergence from policy convergence

statement: The value-of-information (VI) recursion of Section 6.3.3, which trades off exploiting current beliefs about a co-agent's model against exploring actions that reveal information about that model, is a conceptual template for measuring how much an action reduces uncertainty about a teammate's latent policy or skill; however, the book's worked construction uses a fixed, small (two-candidate), known model space and does not address a variable or growing set of co-agents.
section: 6.3.3 Bayesian Learning and Value of Information
conditions: prospective connection only; not evidence about any HMASD-family scenario
limits: the book's VI formalism is defined and demonstrated only for a finite, fixed model space known in advance to the modeling agent
